claims.text: The starting system is zirconium-alloy fuel cladding with a sputter-deposited elemental Cr coating.
CrN and Cr/CrN coatings have previously been considered as protective coating candidates for zirconium-alloy cladding.
The intervention is to form a CrN diffusion barrier within the Cr coating by reactive nitrogen incorporation during deposition.
Reactive sputtering or ion implantation can produce the proposed in-situ CrN barrier in this coating system.
The intervention will produce a continuous and uniform CrN layer approximately 50–150 nm thick at the Cr/zirconium-alloy interface.
CrN is thermodynamically stable over the proposed service conditions.
CrN has sufficiently low diffusivity to function as a diffusion barrier.
An interfacial CrN layer will impede Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Reducing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will mitigate formation of deleterious intermetallic phases.
The CrN barrier will restrict oxygen and steam ingress.
Restricting interdiffusion and oxidant ingress will preserve the integrity and protective function of the Cr coating.
Unmodified Cr coatings can peel and crack during high-temperature steam oxidation.
Cr–Zr interdiffusion causes premature failure of unmodified Cr coatings during high-temperature steam exposure.
Relative to unmodified Cr coating, the Cr/CrN bilayer will reduce interfacial element transport.
Relative to unmodified Cr coating, the Cr/CrN bilayer will reduce oxidation during steam exposure at approximately 1200 °C for about 5 hours.
Relative to unmodified Cr coating, the Cr/CrN bilayer will improve coating integrity during exposure to PWR primary water at approximately 320 °C for tens of days.
The proposed benefits apply across both normal PWR water and accident-relevant high-temperature steam environments.
Long-term reliability under repeated thermal cycling has not yet been established.
